#5030. German Court Offers to Drop Movie2k Case for 40,000 Bitcoin

A Leipzig judge last week offered to dismiss the criminal case against the alleged operator of the defunct Movie2k piracy site if he hands over 40,000 bitcoin, a stake worth about $2.56 billion at current prices. The presiding judge at the Leipzig Regional Court, Karsten Nickel, made the proposal in a trial that began in February.

A spokesman for the Dresden prosecutors’ office confirmed it after German newspapers and the public broadcaster MDR first reported the offer. Heise later published a detailed account.

The trial is before the court’s economic criminal chamber, and the Leipzig court itself had not issued its own confirmation when prosecutors spoke to reporters. Prosecutors believe the defendant still holds about 56,000 bitcoin, and transferring 40,000 would leave him roughly 16,000 coins. At a bitcoin price of about $64,000, those 16,000 coins would be worth about $1.02 billion, and forty thousand bitcoin would be worth about $2.56 billion at the same price. The dollar figures are approximate.

The proposal also calls for him to pay €38 million in compensation for potential victims, including film rights holders, MDR reported. He would also have to give up any claim to the roughly €2.64 billion Saxony already raised from bitcoin he transferred in 2024, the newspaper Freie Presse reported. Even after handing over most of the remaining coins, he could leave court a billionaire.

Movie2k.to ran from 2008 until it was shut down in May 2013. Prosecutors say its operators made millions from advertising contracts and used the proceeds to buy bitcoin when the price was far lower. The defendant is charged with commercial money laundering in 146 cases. The court has already ruled that about 220,000 copyright counts are time-barred and are no longer part of the Movie2k case.

A co-defendant, a Polish national, is charged with money laundering in 46 cases and especially serious tax evasion. Prosecutors say he received bitcoin from the main defendant in May 2013 as pay for work on the site. Nickel has said that proof of some of the charges would face “great difficulties.” It is conceivable, he said, that legally and illegally obtained bitcoin were mixed in the accounts.

German authorities had sought the defendant internationally since late 2019. He was arrested abroad in May 2023 and held in pretrial detention in Saxony until mid-January 2024. On Jan. 16, 2024, he voluntarily transferred about 49,858 bitcoin to wallets provided by the Federal Criminal Police Office. At the time, the coins were worth about €1.96 billion, and he was released from detention around the time of that transfer.

Saxony sold the coins between June 19 and July 12, 2024, with support from the Federal Criminal Police Office, for €2,639,683,413.92, or about €2.64 billion. Prosecutors described the sale as an emergency liquidation required by bitcoin’s volatility. The proceeds are held by the state’s justice treasury and still belong to the defendant until there is a final confiscation ruling. Bitcoin Magazine has covered that sale.

Two other men in the Movie2k investigation were already convicted in 2023 and received suspended sentences. One was a co-operator of the site. The other handled payments.

A co-defendant in the Leipzig trial was offered terms of 600 bitcoin and €17 million, and his lawyer said she could imagine accepting that. The main defendant’s lawyers said they wanted to confer. The Dresden prosecutors’ office and the defense are still reviewing the Movie2k proposal, and neither side has announced a decision.

If both sides agree, the trial could end before Christmas. If they do not, the case will continue, and the court will still have to decide whether to confiscate the 2024 sale proceeds and any bitcoin he still holds.

#5027. Trump’s CFTC picks face Senate scrutiny as prediction market turf war heats up

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

If confirmed, the nominees are likely to face continued scrutiny from lawmakers over the CFTC’s authority to regulate prediction markets.

President Donald Trump’s nominees to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission revealed how they view the hotly contested issue of how to regulate sports betting as the agency continues its pursuit to oversee those markets.

During a Senate Agriculture Committee nomination hearing for Trump's Democratic Party pick, Matthew Rowland and his Republican pick, Nathan Anonick, lawmakers honed in on prediction markets and how the pair would address the agency's regulation of sports betting as states and the federal government butt heads over who should take charge.

"I actually do think the law is quite clear that jurisdiction over sports gambling rests in the hands of states and also with tribes — and yet prediction markets continue to operate, I believe in violation of these state and tribal laws," said Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn.

If confirmed, Anonick and Rowland are likely to face continued scrutiny from lawmakers over the CFTC’s authority to regulate prediction markets, as a growing legal battle over the platforms’ oversight plays out in the courts. Under Chair Michael Selig, the CFTC has asserted that it has "exclusive jurisdiction" over event contracts. Through proposed rulemaking, the CFTC has said that prediction market contracts qualify as swaps because they are based on future events, putting them under federal commodities oversight rather than state gambling laws.

States, meanwhile, argue that prediction market platforms are operating illegal gambling businesses while sidestepping state regulations and tax obligations. Tribal organizations have also raised concerns that the platforms could circumvent existing tribal-state gaming agreements.

Nearly a dozen states and the CFTC have since sued each other, courts have taken opposing sides, and the issue could go all the way to the Supreme Court for a final decision.

During Tuesday's hearing, Rowland pointed to Regulation 40.11, which was adopted by the CFTC in 2011 and prohibits registered exchanges from listing or accepting for clearing certain event contracts involving gaming, terrorism, war and assassination.

"It's hard for me to comment on the active litigation that the CFTC is engaged in, but I'm certainly very sympathetic to the concerns that the states and tribes have raised and would want to work with them further if I were confirmed on that," Rowland added.

However, the term gaming has been the sticking point in whether it is against the public interest.  The CFTC has discretion to decide if a contract is against that public interest, Anonick said, adding that the debate is a "very charged emotional issue," and that he planned to listen to stakeholders.

"I would just argue that, friendly pushback,  that I don't think that this is an emotional issue," Smith said. "I think this is a legal issue."

If confirmed, Anonick and Rowland would join CFTC Chairman Michael Selig, the agency’s sole Republican commissioner. The CFTC and its sister agency, the Securities and Exchange Commission, have faced scrutiny over their failure to fill all five commissioner seats with bipartisan representation over the past year

Next, the Senate Agriculture Committee would have to vote on the nominees before that heads to a full Senate vote. Timing is tight ahead of a new Congress in January, and nominations would generally have to be resubmitted.

#5024. Former Robinhood Engineer Pleads Guilty to Crypto Insider Trading Scheme

Former Robinhood Engineer Pleads Guilty to Crypto Insider Trading Scheme

Former Robinhood software engineer Huaisong “Jerry” Xiang pleaded guilty Monday to wire fraud for using confidential plans for upcoming cryptocurrency listings to trade on Hyperliquid. The 30-year-old agreed to forfeit $125,523 in profits from the scheme, according to the Justice Department.

Xiang entered his plea before U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon on November 16, two months after prosecutors accused him and another Robinhood engineer of trading ahead of the brokerage's token announcements. He pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud; the DOJ announcement did not report a guilty plea to the commodities-fraud charge initially brought against him.

As a software engineer working on new listings for Robinhood Crypto, Xiang had access to a private Slack channel reserved for employees classified as “Coin Aware Individuals.” It contained information about which tokens were coming to the platform and when, according to the FBI complaint filed in September.

Robinhood's internal policy prohibited that group from trading around upcoming listings on any platform, not just Robinhood. The restriction began before a listing was announced and continued for 24 hours after it became public. A November 2024 email warned Xiang to “refrain from abusing access to or knowledge of this information,” the complaint says.

Investigators described one trade involving POPCAT, a Solana-based meme coin. After receiving internal messages about a planned March 13, 2025 listing, Xiang moved approximately 18 Ethereum, then worth about $34,000, into a Hyperliquid wallet and opened a bullish position tied to POPCAT, according to the complaint.

He closed that position at a profit after the token became available on Robinhood but before the company published its listing announcement, the FBI alleged. The complaint identified at least 10 other occasions through February 2026 when the same wallet traded ahead of announcements, including positions involving MEW, MOODENG, ONDO and RENDER.

Hyperliquid's perpetual futures let traders speculate on a cryptocurrency's price without owning the token itself. Unlike conventional futures, the contracts have no expiration date, and a “long” position gains value if the underlying token's price rises.

New listings can increase a token's exposure to buyers and put upward pressure on its price. Prosecutors said Xiang used his advance knowledge to position himself for those moves, sometimes closing his trades before the public knew Robinhood had added the asset.

“No matter the trading platform, corporate insiders will be held accountable when they trade based on misappropriated information,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in Monday's announcement.

Robinhood said in September that it had investigated the matter, reported it to authorities and maintained a zero-tolerance policy on insider trading.

Xiang faces a statutory maximum of 20 years in prison, although the judge will decide his sentence. He is scheduled to appear before McMahon for sentencing on February 25, 2027.

#5023. Ionic Digital (IOND) Sells 737 Bitcoin to Fund Data Center Buildout

Ionic Digital (IOND) sold about 737 bitcoin after the end of September for roughly $61.6 million and plans to spend the money building out its data center sites, the miner built from Celsius’ old mining business disclosed in its latest quarterly report. The company said in its 10-Q that the coins sold at an average of $83,600 each, net of trading costs. The sales cut its bitcoin holdings by about 25% from the Sept. 30 balance.

Ionic held 2,954 bitcoin at the end of the third quarter, up from 2,719 at the end of 2025. That implies about 2,217 bitcoin left after the sales. “The Company intends to use the proceeds to fund the development of its existing data center sites,” the filing said.

The filing does not say when the coins were sold. Bitcoin traded near $64,000 on Wednesday morning, about 23% below Ionic’s average sale price.

Ionic was formed in January 2024 to take over the assets of Celsius Mining under the bankrupt lender’s Chapter 11 plan. It started out as a pure bitcoin miner, running fleets of ASIC machines at its own and hosted sites. That changed in October 2025, when it signed a lease with a single tenant for its Ward County, Texas, facility, which it previously called Cedarvale. The lease runs through January 2037.

The third quarter shows how far the shift has gone, with revenue rising to about $49.0 million from $37.1 million a year earlier. Digital infrastructure leasing brought in $43.9 million of that, while mining revenue fell to $5.1 million from $37.1 million.

Ionic swung to a net profit of $17.4 million for the quarter, compared with a $4.5 million loss a year earlier. That result included a $73.2 million gain on the fair value of its bitcoin, offset in part by a $65.9 million loss from remeasuring warrants. For the first nine months of the year, Ionic posted a net loss of $30.9 million.

In February, Ionic amended the Ward County lease. The tenant is now obligated to lease another 89 megawatts of capacity when it becomes available. Control of that added capacity had not passed to the tenant by the end of September, so Ionic has not booked any revenue on it. The company also had about $19.6 million left to pay on transformer purchases and a substation expansion at the site.

The conversion has cost Ionic mining capacity. The company said it does not have room at its owned and leased sites to relocate all of the miners it used to run, so it has decommissioned some of them. Ionic went public through a direct listing on July 28 and raised $400 million in a private placement before $16.7 million in costs. It had about $381.4 million in cash and equivalents at Sept. 30.

Ionic is one of several public miners turning bitcoin into cash for AI and data center projects this month. MARA sold 13,597 bitcoin for $1.1 billion and said more sales were coming. Core Scientific plans to exit bitcoin mining by year-end, and Hyperscale Data sold its last bitcoin to fund an AI data center.

Ionic’s sale is smaller, but the share is large. A quarter of its treasury is now going into the data center buildout. The company still mines. In July, it moved its hashrate from Foundry to Luxor’s mining pool, and mining added about $5.1 million worth of bitcoin to its holdings in the third quarter.

The test now is whether the 89 megawatts come online fast enough to justify selling coins that would fetch about $14 million less at Wednesday’s price.

#5021. What’s happening to crypto startup valuations?

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Sign up to get 2 days early access to each edition of The Funding

Last month, Axios reported, citing multiple sources, that Visa was in late-stage talks to acquire Fireblocks for about $2.5 billion. That's less than a third of the $8 billion valuation Fireblocks reached in January 2022. Fireblocks denied the report, telling The Block, "This is news to us, and not true at present time."

Regardless of the denial, the reported price brings up the question of how much private crypto companies are worth now, particularly those that raised capital during the 2021-22 boom.

Sources said the reported Fireblocks price is not far from what they have been seeing in secondary markets, whether or not Visa ends up buying the company.

"On our network, 2021-22 infrastructure supply has been quoted 60% to 70% under the last round for over a year," said Omar-Shakeeb Zahir, co-founder and CEO of SecondLane, a crypto secondary market platform. "A $2.5 billion figure against $8 billion sits right in that range."

A number of crypto companies haven't raised new funding since 2021 or 2022, so their last reported valuations are outdated. But shares sold by investors and employees in secondary markets are now going for much lower prices.

"A 2021 round is worth about 40 cents on the dollar today," Zahir said.

Jonas Thiele, founder and CEO of crypto secondary market platform OFFX, also said shares of well-known 2021-22 unicorns are regularly offered at discounts of 50% to 70%, "and for some of the biggest names of that cycle it's closer to 90%."

Karl-Martin Ahrend, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment banking and M&A advisory firm Areta, estimated discounts of 50% to 80% across secondary markets and M&A. Thomas Klocanas, managing partner at Strobe Ventures, said secondary prices for late-stage companies from 2021 are generally 40% to 70% below their last rounds, "often with no clearing bid at all."

Data from secondary markets is helpful because many companies haven't had a new funding round to establish a lower valuation. Of the 49 companies in Architect Partners' database that raised at valuations of $1 billion or more in 2021 and 2022, 25 haven't announced another financing, said Adlee Heshmat, senior financial analyst at Architect Partners, a crypto investment bank and M&A advisor.

"Down rounds aren't really announced," Heshmat said, adding: "The repricing tends to show up in secondaries and in M&A, where buyers are pricing off of today's revenue, strategic fit and public company multiples."

Some crypto companies are still getting much higher valuations than in the past, especially in payments, stablecoins, trading and prediction markets. But many companies that raised at the 2021 peak are now trading at large discounts to their last funding rounds.

"It's a two-speed market. Most companies that raised at the 2021-22 peak trade well below those rounds today," Thiele said. "What holds up is anything with real revenue and a regulatory moat."

Heshmat made a similar point, saying, "It's a two-tier market right now. At the very top, valuations are now above the 2021-22 peak." Since last November, Architect Partners has tracked eight funding rounds at valuations of $20 billion or more, involving Ripple, Kraken, Kalshi, Polymarket, Crypto.com and OKX.

Only one company reached that level in 2021 and 2022, Heshmat said. He didn't name the company, but it was likely FTX, which raised at a $32 billion valuation in early 2022 before collapsing that November.

"Below that, late-stage valuations are still about a third under early 2022 averages," Heshmat added.

Payments and stablecoin companies have raised 39% more funding this year than at the same point in 2022, while funding for NFTs, gaming, protocols and developer tools is down around 80%, according to Heshmat.

The sources pointed to revenue as one of the main reasons some companies are doing better than others.

"There isn't one private crypto market anymore. There are two, and they barely talk to each other," Klocanas said. "Businesses with revenue, licenses and real distribution are at or above 2021 levels. The token-first infrastructure of the last cycle is the opposite," he added.

Klocanas said stablecoin payments, onchain credit, regulated trading and tokenization are doing better than other crypto sectors. General-purpose Layer 1 and Layer 2 blockchains, middleware companies with no revenue and consumer apps that depend on token incentives have struggled.

Prediction markets are one area where valuations have risen sharply, with Kalshi and Polymarket among the biggest players.

Ahrend said there are only a few major prediction market companies, and their valuations depend on whether they can stay ahead of competitors. On stablecoins, he said valuations "are justified for the few leaders with real volume, licenses and distribution, not for the long tail."

Klocanas agreed, saying: "The category leaders can grow into those numbers. The fifteenth stablecoin orchestration startup raising at 50x ARR [annual recurring revenue] probably can't."

The sources I spoke with said valuations were so high in 2021 largely because crypto markets were booming at the time.

"The 2021 rounds were priced in a hype phase," OFFX's Thiele said. "Crypto was a young market, trading volumes were at record highs, and investors were willing to pay for growth almost at any price."

Zahir said interest rates were near zero when those rounds took place. Valuation multiples were also high, and much of the revenue came from trading activity and token prices. Investors were expecting that growth to continue.

"Rates rose, multiples came back to earth, and much of that revenue never grew into the valuation," he said.

Lex Sokolin, co-founder and managing partner at Generative Ventures, said, "Multiple compression is at play — from 50x to 10x as growth stalls."

Thiele said many companies are still good businesses, "some much better than in 2021. But the price was set at the top of the cycle, and a company doesn't stay worth its peak valuation just because that was the last round."

Funds are also looking to get cash back from their investments, even if they have to sell shares for less than their last funding round prices. Founders also have to decide whether to wait for better prices or sell at current valuations.

"Funds now need DPI [distributions to paid-in capital], not TVPI [total value to paid-in capital]: cash at half the last round beats a paper 1x that never converts," Ahrend said.

Zahir also said, "LPs now judge on DPI, so GPs will use secondaries to sell parts of their winners and take the discount on the tail."

Some funds and early employees have already started selling their shares at discounts instead of waiting for the market to recover.

"For them, liquidity today is often worth more than a higher mark that may never be realized," Thiele said.

He added that founders must decide "whether to wait for the market to grow back into the old valuation or to accept a realistic price now."

Ahrend advised founders to start looking for buyers early. "Businesses are bought, not sold. Start a process with 18 months of runway, not six."

The sources I spoke to don't expect to see valuations across the crypto market returning to their 2021 highs. Though more exits that return cash to investors, clearer regulations, and revenue that can hold up when crypto prices fall could help some companies recover.

A few major IPOs and acquisitions could also help the market establish more realistic valuations.

"A few clean IPOs and strategic sales at sensible prices would reset the reference points for the whole market, more than any new funding round could," Thiele said.

Regulation is another factor. Stablecoins now have a U.S. law, but the crypto market structure bill stalled in the Senate in September, and with Democrats taking back control of the House and the Senate, the chances of further crypto legislation during President Donald Trump's second term are slim. Despite that, Klocanas said institutions need "predictability more than a single statute."

As for what could help valuations recover, Thiele said companies need revenue "that doesn't depend on token prices or trading volumes," while Sokolin said crypto businesses need to "challenge banks for their core money and lending offerings, or their capital markets venues."

Still, Ahrend expects many of the companies that raised during the 2021 boom to be acquired, recapitalized or shut down.

"Most of the 2021 class won't see peak marks again and will be resolved through M&A, recaps or wind-downs," Ahrend said. "2027 looks like a consolidation year."

Klocanas said returning to 2021 prices shouldn't be the goal. "We don't expect a broad recovery to 2021 levels, and in fact I don't think we should want one," he said. "What's ahead is a market that prices crypto companies like fintech and market infrastructure companies, on revenue, regulatory moat and distribution."

#5019. Coinbase AI defense blocks $4.7 million from being sent to deepfake Elon Musk scam

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The company said the system prevented about 91% of the attempted transfers linked to the fake Tesla livestream, with no human intervention.

Coinbase Coinbase Global, Inc. (COIN) said its AI-powered scam defenses stopped $4.7 million in funds that customers tried to send to scammers who used an Elon Musk deepfake to promote a fake Tesla crypto giveaway in a livestream. The company said the system prevented about 91% of the attempted transfers, with no humans in the loop.

According to Coinbase's blog post published on Tuesday, the incident occurred during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration last month. Scammers created a YouTube livestream that resembled Tesla's official broadcast, featuring a deepfake of Elon Musk. It also featured on-screen wallet addresses and a QR code, offering to double any cryptocurrency sent. More than 500,000 people watched the stream, according to Coinbase.

Within roughly two hours, hundreds of Coinbase customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the addresses shown.

"The part that makes this hard: nobody was hacked," Coinbase said. "No Coinbase account was broken into, no password stolen, no credential phished. Hundreds of customers, many of them long-time users, decided on their own to send money to a stranger."

While most platforms have adopted real-time fraud detection systems, Coinbase explained that it is difficult for them to stop transactions that customers were actually tricked into authorizing.

Coinbase said its AI defense system closed that loophole by flagging the activity in real time using machine-learning models that score risky sends, including those matching giveaway patterns, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses.

Then, it dispatched a dedicated scam-prevention agent to examine the context of the transaction, explain how the scams are structured, and ask questions that deconstruct the story scammers were pitching.

"What's notable is that the agent had never seen this scam. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch weren't in its training," Coinbase said. "It recognized the shape of the scheme anyway, a promise to multiply funds, the urgency of an event that would end in hours, a transfer that could not be reversed, and it ran from the first flagged send to the last, with no humans in the loop."

Coinbase said it will continue to invest heavily in AI defense to create models that keep pace with new scam types through AI-driven research.

#5018. Analyst: Bitcoin Below $70,000 is a ‘Gift From the Market’

K33 Research said bitcoin is trading in “deep value territory” after a 14% weekly drop, arguing that “any entry below $70K is a gift from the market” for medium- to long-term investors.

The call comes in the firm’s weekly report, “No gain, plenty of pain,” which published Nov. 16. Head of research Vetle Lunde wrote that bitcoin’s slide has erased its August and September gains and left the market deeply oversold. Bitcoin has posted six straight red weekly candles and is on track for a record 13 consecutive days of lower daily highs, according to K33.

Lunde said a streak of six weekly losses has happened only twice before, from Jan. 26 to March 1, 2026, and from April 3 to May 29, 2022. Daily RSI, a momentum gauge, hit 19.95 on Saturday and has stayed below 25 since Friday. Bitcoin also fell below its 200-week moving average, near $68,000, after its worst weekly return since June 7.

At the bottom on Nov. 15, bitcoin traded about 8.5% under the 200-week average, a wider gap than the 7.3% recorded at June’s low of $58,500. K33 said 51.5% of the bitcoin supply last moved on-chain at prices above the current level, meaning the average holder could have sold for more at some point in the past four years.

Lunde said those readings, taken together, have typically lined up with market bottoms. K33 also noted that crypto has lagged traditional markets, with the Nasdaq and S&P 500 recovering modestly last week while bitcoin sank.

Bitcoin was trading near $62,300 on Wednesday, according to Coinbase spot prices, below the roughly $65,000 level cited in the K33 report, which showed bitcoin down 14% on the week and about 20% over 30 days. Ether also fell 14% over the week, to around $1,827.

Capital continues to leave bitcoin funds. Net outflows from bitcoin exchange-traded products reached 44,900 BTC over the 14 trading days since Oct. 29, K33 said, short of the record of about 71,000 BTC set in June. Total ETF holdings fell to about 1.46 million BTC, the lowest since Aug. 19, and leveraged ETF exposure dropped to 21,900 BTC, the lowest since March 2024.

Forced selling hit derivatives, too. About $1.3 billion in long positions were liquidated on Nov. 13 and 14 as bitcoin broke below $70,000, K33 said, and funding rates on perpetual futures repeatedly turned negative. Open interest fell by about 30,000 BTC but stayed above 330,000 BTC, leaving leverage elevated against historical norms.

Institutional futures players largely stayed on the sidelines. Open interest in bitcoin futures on CME stayed below 100,000 BTC all week, K33 said, a sign that regulated-market participants have not rushed in to buy the dip.

Demand for downside protection is also surging. The one-month 25-delta skew, which compares the price of puts to calls, rose above 20 for the first time since July, a level Lunde said has historically coincided with “selling exhaustion near local bottoms.”

Stablecoins offer another sign of stress. K33 said net redemptions totaled $16.1 billion over the past month, the largest outflow since the collapse of Terra.

Lunde stopped short of calling the decline over. He said earlier recoveries from similar conditions involved “prolonged consolidation,” pointing to a choppy recovery rather than an immediate rebound.

There were some constructive signs in trading activity. Spot volume ran near $5 billion a day from Friday through Sunday, the busiest weekend since February, which K33 said could give the market firmer footing after weeks of one-way selling.

Even so, leverage remains high, and ETF money is still heading out the door. Bitcoin was near $62,300 at the time of writing, below the roughly $68,000 200-week average K33 flagged as a key level.

#5015. Binance Hack Wallets Move $137 Million in Ethereum After Two Weeks of Silence

Binance Hack Wallets Move $137 Million in Ethereum After Two Weeks of Silence

Wallets linked to the $6.3 billion Binance hack started moving large amounts of stolen Ethereum on Tuesday, breaking more than two weeks of inactivity as U.S. authorities continue trying to recover the funds.

Blockchain security service MistTrack reported that one address associated with the October 29 theft sent 34,279.66 ETH, worth roughly $63 million at the time, to three newly created wallets. The address had not moved its funds since October 30.

The on-chain record shows three outgoing transactions shortly before 7 a.m. UTC: two transfers of 12,000 ETH ($21.2 million) each and a third of about 10,279.66 ETH ($18.2 million). MistTrack said the receiving wallets had not sent the ether onward when it posted its initial alert.

That $63 million movement was only part of Tuesday’s activity. A second wallet linked to the same hack transferred another 40,600.66 ETH, worth roughly $74 million, across five transactions.

Analytics firm Arkham shows wallets linked to the attack had transferred a combined 74,880 ETH, valued at $136.8 million, over roughly three hours, and funds were beginning to be swapped for Bitcoin through Thorchain, a service that moves and exchanges crypto between blockchains.

The transfers come five days after the Justice Department said courts had authorized it to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion connected to the Binance theft. That sum is part of more than $2.7 billion frozen through combined government and private-sector action, not an additional recovery on top of it.

The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a hacking operation it links to North Korea’s military. The October 29 breach drained roughly $6.43 billion from Binance across 11 blockchains, according to blockchain analytics company Elliptic, making it the largest known crypto theft. North Korea denied involvement.

The attackers rushed to convert stablecoins into assets their issuers could not freeze. Tether and Circle can block stolen tokens on their networks, but ordinary ETH and Bitcoin do not have a central company capable of stopping a particular wallet from sending them.

Elliptic’s November 16 analysis put the frozen or seized portion at $2.85 billion and said the main Bitcoin and ETH holdings were still sitting in attack-linked addresses. That was before Tuesday’s transfers, which show at least part of the previously stationary ETH has begun moving.

The attackers had also spread their activity across almost 27,000 wallets and more than 83,000 transactions. That complicated trail does not mean they have managed to turn most of the stolen assets into cash.

Elliptic said only a negligible amount had likely been cashed out as of its latest assessment. To do that at scale, the holders would typically need an exchange or an over-the-counter broker willing to take the funds, creating another point at which authorities could identify and potentially block them.

The initiative plans to initially focus on an intermediated and interoperable stablecoin-based payment model, with participation from borrower countries.

The World Bank Group (WBG) said it is exploring the use of regulated USD stablecoins with Citi and Circle to speed up and cut the cost of fund disbursements.

In a statement released Tuesday, the international organization said that it plans to test blockchain-based payment rails alongside traditional correspondent banking to improve existing WBG funds disbursement arrangements.

"This initiative is about exploring ways to make the financial plumbing of development work better for the people who need it most," WBG President Ajay Banga said in the statement. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said it is building an internet-native financial system, and "development finance is one of its most important applications."

"Money that moves at the speed of the internet shouldn't be reserved for the world's biggest banks and corporations; it should reach the people and places that need it most, with full visibility into where every dollar goes," Allaire added.

The World Bank Group is a multilateral development institution owned by 189 member countries. It comprises five organizations that work to reduce poverty and support sustainable growth in developing economies.

In the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, the group delivered $123.5 billion in loans, grants, equity investments, and guarantees to partner countries and private businesses, according to its latest annual report. This includes $35.8 billion in Sub-Saharan Africa, $25.1 billion in Latin America and the Caribbean, and $24.6 billion in Europe and Central Asia.

#5011. Binance Says It Won Court Order to Recover Frozen Hack Funds

Binance says it has secured a court order from Abu Dhabi Global Market to help it recover crypto frozen after the record $6.3 billion hack last month, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The exchange has not said how much of the money the order covers.

Reuters described Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) as Binance’s main financial regulator. Binance deputy general counsel Dugan Bliss confirmed the order in a statement but gave no details on its terms. Neither the company nor Reuters said which assets it applies to.

“We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers,” Bliss said.

Binance has said about $2.85 billion of the stolen tokens were frozen or intercepted after the Oct. 29 attack, according to its own incident report. That is roughly 45% of the $6.34 billion it says was affected.

Most of it sits with stablecoin issuers. Tether said it froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT within 30 minutes of the attack, and Circle said it froze about $1.1 billion in USDC in coordination with law enforcement. Circle added that it does not decide who owns frozen assets, a question it left to law enforcement and the courts.

The Justice Department has separately obtained court authority to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen crypto. It is part of more than $2.7 billion that Justice says government and private-sector efforts have frozen. Criminal Division head A. Tysen Duva said the department helped “immediately halt about half of this historic breach.” Reuters did not say how the ADGM order fits with the U.S. action.

Binance says the attack began months earlier, with a tampered software installer that compromised one engineer in June. In September, another engineer was approached by a fake recruiter and persuaded to run a bogus interview assignment that installed malware, the company said.

From there, the attackers reached an internal wallet-signing service and drained Binance hot wallets across multiple blockchains on Oct. 29. The thefts included 233.46 million XRP, about 970,500 SOL and 18,270 BTC, according to Binance.

The FBI has attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and Binance has said the same. Pyongyang denies involvement. Blockchain analysts said the attacker tried to outrun the freezes by swapping stablecoins into ether over about 20 minutes, but the issuers moved faster.

That split matters for bitcoin. Tether and Circle can block their own tokens, but bitcoin has no issuer. The stolen BTC is not covered by those freezes and can be stopped only if it reaches an exchange or service that blocks it.

Binance has already said it replaced the affected assets with company funds, using part of its SAFU emergency fund and its corporate treasury. Withdrawals resumed in phases earlier this month, and the exchange aims to reopen all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week, Reuters reported.

On Wednesday, Binance’s Asia-Pacific head SB Seker told Reuters at the Singapore FinTech Festival that the company plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027 and does not need to raise new funds. He said talks are under way with five or six markets, three of them at a mature stage, and details are due in the first quarter.

Seker said the cost of replacing the stolen tokens was “statistically” not a large amount for the company. “In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate,” he said.

#5007. Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as Nvidia CEO, publicly addressing the campaign to reinstate him less than a week after his abrupt departure. His offer came despite reports that the chipmaker's board has no plans to bring him back.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote in a statement on X.

The Nvidia co-founder also apologized for the conduct that triggered his exit. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he wrote. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.”

“I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he added.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…

— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026

His X profile underwent a separate change around the same time. By Tuesday, Huang had removed “CEO” from his bio, which now identifies him only as “Founder of NVIDIA”; the company banner and corporate affiliation badge also disappeared.

Huang resigned last Thursday after 33 years leading the chipmaker he founded in 1993. His departure followed disclosures about extramarital relationships involving Nvidia employees and a business executive whom U.S. officials suspect of connections to Chinese intelligence. Those intelligence allegations have not been established as fact.

The board's independent investigation is examining his conduct and whether sensitive company information or national security were put at risk. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised; chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. He said many were reaching out directly as Nvidia navigates “complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” he added.

But the board's position—at least as of Tuesday—is that directors are focused on the investigation, not reinstatement.

The company is simultaneously looking for a successor. Directors reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive, according to the Financial Times, although Nvidia said it had not formally engaged candidates and called speculation premature.

The movement to restore Huang has nevertheless attracted powerful allies. President Donald Trump said Monday he “would certainly not mind” a comeback, while Elon Musk backed a petition demanding Huang's reinstatement that had drawn nearly 192,000 signatures by Monday.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman offered a more qualified defense. Altman, who was briefly fired and reinstated at OpenAI in 2023, said Huang had “long been a hero of mine” and that “heroes have flaws,” but stopped short of saying Nvidia should rehire him.

Huang also made a patriotic appeal, especially considering his outsting was especially rushed not because of his affairs but because of the possibility of him leaking secrets to China. “I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life,” he wrote.

“NVIDIA has been my life’s work,” he continued. “Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.”

He closed by thanking supporters and telling his family, “I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.” Nvidia, meanwhile, is continuing its permanent CEO search, with Kress scheduled to lead the company's quarterly earnings call later today.

#5005. Lighter incident exposes risks beyond withdrawal controls

Crypto platforms need enforceable limits on every route an API key can use to transfer value, including trades, internal transfers and shared pools.

A recent incident where over $10 million was siphoned out of a decentralized perpetual futures exchange shows the shortcomings of focusing security on withdrawal controls

According to Lighter’s postmortem, an attacker used compromised API keys to move funds into a public pool and redeem shares held through another account. Bitquery traced a withdrawal of 10.39 million USDC. The exchange said its protocol and smart contracts were unaffected.

Lighter now requires wallet signatures for transfers into public pools and has made API-key signatures non-public. It also plans IP allowlists and configurable permissions for individual keys.

Lighter has since restored deposits and withdrawals while also returning about $5 million in USDC (USDC) to the affected trader.

Lighter incident infographic. Source: Bitquery

The incident highlights how cybersecurity reviews need to look past smart contract vulnerabilities. It is important to also consider the gap between the permissions a system grants and the financial consequences those permissions allow.

Related: Google says hackers use AI agents to find and exploit software flaws

The real risk involving a credential depends on the balances it can reach, the transactions it can initiate and the exposures it can create. Whether it is permitted to withdraw assets and to which destinations are just two of many factors. As Lighter put it in its postmortem:

This means that a user needs to establish a clear mandate for each credential. The mandate can specify accessible accounts, permitted markets, order sizes, pricing tolerances and aggregate exposure. Moving capital into a shared pool or expanding those limits can require separate authorization.

The same logic applies to additional signatures. A second signature adds meaningful protection when its approval process independently evaluates the transaction’s financial effect.

#5004. Scattered Spider Hacker Gets Six Years for $11.6 Million Crypto Theft

A Scottish hacker tied to the Scattered Spider group was sentenced to six years in U.S. federal prison on Tuesday for a text-message phishing and SIM-swapping scheme that stole at least $11.6 million in crypto, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California said.

Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, received a 72-month sentence from U.S. District Judge John W. Holcomb in Santa Ana. He had pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. A restitution hearing is set for Dec. 11.

Prosecutors did not say which cryptocurrencies were taken, and the release does not break the haul down by coin. Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in the case, closing out a prosecution of a hacker crew that the Justice Department charged together.

From September 2021 to April 2023, Buchanan and his co-conspirators sent hundreds of phishing texts to employees of at least a dozen companies, prosecutors said. The messages posed as the employer or one of its IT contractors and linked to fake login pages that captured usernames, passwords and other personal information.

The group then used the stolen data to run SIM swaps, which move a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the attacker controls. That gave them a way into victims’ virtual currency accounts and wallets. The BBC reported that Buchanan set up a Telegram bot to collect the credentials as workers handed them over.

The largest single theft, according to prosecutors, was $1.67 million taken from one victim in December 2022. Prosecutors said the thefts had “severe, life-altering consequences” for victims.

The BBC said the money came from individual victims rather than from the companies whose employees were phished. Prosecutors first put the hacker group’s take at about $8 million, and the $11.6 million figure is the loss authorities calculated for the full scheme.

Police Scotland searched Buchanan’s bedroom in April 2023 after a request from the FBI, the BBC said. Investigators found a device holding the names and addresses of victims, along with crypto seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.

Buchanan left the U.K. the following month. Spanish authorities arrested him at Palma de Mallorca Airport in 2024 as he tried to board a private flight to Naples.

Bloomberg News reported, and Reuters relayed, that he was extradited from Spain in April 2025. He was charged with wire fraud and aggravated identity theft alongside four other alleged Scattered Spider members, and he has been in U.S. custody since.

Reuters has described Scattered Spider as a loose-knit community of hackers suspected of breaking into dozens of U.S. companies. The DOJ release does not use the group’s name, but the BBC says Buchanan, a teenage hacker when the campaign began, was a member and a Justice Department spokesperson has previously tied the defendants to it.

The BBC said Buchanan’s four co-defendants have all pleaded guilty and are serving time. It described the case as a years-long investigation involving authorities in the U.K., the U.S., Spain and Canada.

Scattered Spider has also faced prosecution in Britain. Two other members were jailed in the U.K. in July for a series of attacks, including one on Transport for London that caused £39 million in damage, the BBC said.

The judge will set the amount of restitution at a hearing on Dec. 11, the final step in the case against the Scottish hacker.

TD Cowen on Wednesday maintained its Buy rating on Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) treasury company Sharplink SharpLink Inc. (SBET) and kept its price target at $13.

Senior Analyst Lance Vitanza said the firm is taking a more conservative view of ether’s price path after observing a sharp drop in ETH burn per transaction, even as network activity continues to grow.

TD Cowen now assumes ether ends the fourth quarter of 2026 at approximately $2,413, down 10% quarter-over-quarter from the third quarter, with a flatter appreciation trajectory thereafter.

“Ethereum activity remains robust, but more transactions are producing materially less ETH burn, prompting a more conservative price outlook," Vitanza wrote. "The flatter appreciation profile is deliberate. We remain constructive on Ethereum adoption but now place greater emphasis on declining ETH burn per transaction."

At the same time, he noted that Sharplink’s shift toward more active treasury management could generate incremental ether-denominated returns.

Sharplink's holdings rose from 892,708 ETH by the end of the third quarter to 896,003 ETH as of Nov. 16, with the recent increase coming primarily from staking rewards and related yield rather than new purchases. Cumulative staking rewards reached 31,820 ETH.

The treasury firm's management has also deployed capital into liquid staking via a $200 million allocation to Lido and into the Galaxy Sharplink Onchain Yield Fund.

"We view these initiatives as potentially important sources of incremental ETH-denominated return and an increasingly differentiated part of the Sharplink story," the note said. "For now, however, we largely leave that potential upside unmodeled."

In the case of a favorable ether price environment, the TD Cowen analyst said he expects Sharplink to "substantially outperform" spot ether exchange-traded products by increasing its holdings of ether per fully-diluted share. If ether price remains depressed, Vitanza said the company's staking yield should be more than enough to fully cover operating costs.

Sharplink reported third-quarter net income of $751.4 million, or $3.45 per diluted share, compared with $104.3 million a year earlier, driven largely by $676.7 million in unrealized gains on its ether holdings. Revenue rose 24% year over year to $13.5 million, almost entirely from staking income of $13.1 million.

Its CEO Joseph Chalom said the company is focused on “maximizing the productivity of our ETH holdings” while maintaining disciplined capital allocation.

"Our relentless focus translates into tangible financial results, highlighted by double-digit revenue growth, improved operating leverage and a material increase in net income," Chalom added.

#4997. Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade threatens to break as many as 15,000 smart contracts, developers warned during a core developer call Monday, forcing a debate over how much disruption the network should tolerate in the name of scaling.

The concern centers on two proposed changes, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, designed to let Ethereum scale from 60 million gas to as much as 200 million gas per block, a roughly 3.3x jump that developers say would sharply lower costs for most users while keeping state growth in check.

The problem, flagged late in the development process, is that the changes break certain invariants, assumptions that some smart contracts were built to rely on.

“Multiple contracts were relying on invariants in the protocol that are modified by 8037 and 8038,” said Marius van der Wijden, an Ethereum Foundation developer who worked on the scaling effort.

He acknowledged that the team “wanted to do significant public outreach” but that timelines slipped amid reorganizations and budget cuts at the foundation. He said he shares “a lot of blame” as the last remaining scaling lead still at the EF.

Two security firms, ChainSecurity and Dedaub, presented findings from AI-assisted audits, with the combined search turning up roughly 200 distinct classes of affected contracts, most tied to gas-cost increases rather than the new mechanics themselves.

Van der Wijden put the highest estimate at 10,000 to 15,000 contracts, a “fringe subset” of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million, with impacted value he loosely pegged in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars among contracts not yet committed to upgrading.

App developers pushed back on the framing. Jango, who builds the Juicebox protocol, warned the change undermines “composability,” a core Ethereum value prop, and shakes “developer confidence in building immutable protocols.” A Uniswap developer urged that EIP-8037 “should definitely be reconsidered.”

The Ethereum Foundation already delayed Glamsterdam’s testnet fork over these gas-related security flaws. Developers stressed Monday that no decision has been made, with the question headed to Thursday’s execution-layer call.

But several signaled a strong desire to ship the fork as planned, arguing that removing the changes could delay Glamsterdam, and the broader roadmap toward post-quantum security, by four to six months, time they say Ethereum can’t spare as quantum and AI threats loom.

#4996. Eastern Europe crypto flows fall 7.9% as Ukraine draws $12B in stablecoins

Chainalysis found that Eastern Europe recorded the steepest decline in crypto activity of any region, while cross-border stablecoin transfers to Ukraine continued amid the ongoing war.

Eastern Europe recorded the steepest decline in cryptocurrency activity among the regions tracked by Chainalysis in the year ended June 2026, falling 7.9% even as retail-sized transfers increased in value, according to a report published Tuesday.

The region’s crypto economy shrank to $642.1 billion from $697.1 billion a year earlier, compared with a 1.6% decline globally, the report states. Russia, which accounted for roughly 44% of the regional total, saw activity fall 14.7% to $284.1 billion over the period. By contrast, Belarus recorded 27.6% growth, while Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine saw smaller increases.

The value of transfers of $10,000 or more to crypto services fell 17.4%, from $591.5 billion to $488.6 billion, according to the report.

The value of smaller transfers to crypto services, meanwhile, rose 8.3%. These retail-sized transfers accounted for 13.1% of the value sent to crypto services in Eastern Europe, the highest share of any region studied and above the global average of 10.1%.

Eastern European crypto activity by country, July 2025 to June 2026. Source: Chainalysis report

Crypto ATM activity also increased across Eastern Europe, with transaction volumes nearly doubling from $17.3 million to $33.9 million. Poland recorded a 120% increase in ATM transactions despite a 5% decline in centralized exchange activity, with stablecoins accounting for roughly 90% of its ATM transactions.

Chainalysis measures the crypto economy using inflows to crypto services, domestic transfers between personal wallets and cross-border inflows to personal wallets. The figures are measured in dollars, so cryptocurrency price changes can also affect the totals, according to its methodology.

Related: OpenPayd secures MiCA license as stablecoin adoption grows in Europe

Despite the broader regional decline, Ukraine remained a major destination for stablecoins, receiving $12 billion in cross-border wallet-to-wallet transfers. Of that, $2.41 billion was in retail-sized transfers below $10,000, according to Chainalysis.

Chainalysis also found that countries with larger Ukrainian populations, including prewar diaspora communities and refugees who arrived after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, generally sent more stablecoins to Ukraine. Among the 36 countries studied across Europe and North America,

Canada was the largest source of retail-sized, remittance-like transfers, at $359 million.

Crypto transfers to Ukraine by diaspora population, July 2025 to June 2026. Source: Chainalysis report

A Chainalysis spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the cross-border flows were largely denominated in US dollar-pegged stablecoins, although the firm did not provide a breakdown by individual token.

K33's Vetle Lunde said bitcoin was an attractive buy below $70,000, while Glassnode said buying demand remains thin.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) fell 14% over the past week following six straight weekly losses, a streak analysts at research and brokerage firm K33 said has only been witnessed twice before, between Jan. 26 and March 1, 2026, and from April 3 to May 29, 2022.

"BTC is now deeply oversold, with daily RSI reaching 19.95 on Saturday and remaining below 25 since Friday. Furthermore, BTC has fallen below its 200-week moving average after recording its worst weekly return since June 7," K33 Head of Research Vetle Lunde noted in a new report.

At one point during the selloff, bitcoin was about 8.5% below its 200-week moving average, a deeper deviation than the 7.3% recorded at June's $58,500 lows, he noted, adding that 51.5% of circulating bitcoin is now held at a loss.

"Any entry below $70K is a gift from the market," Lunde said. "Together, these signals suggest BTC is trading in deep value territory, offering an attractive buying opportunity for medium- to long-term investors. Such conditions have typically been associated with market bottoms."

Meanwhile, in the options market, demand for downside protection pushed the one-month 25-delta skew above 20 for the first time since July, according to K33. "Similar levels have historically coincided with selling exhaustion near local bottoms," Lunde wrote. However, he said previous recoveries from similar levels had involved "prolonged consolidation," suggesting a choppy recovery rather than an immediate rebound.

Bitcoin is currently trading for around $64,000 on Wednesday, down 1.1% over the past 24 hours, after setting a record 13 consecutive days of lower daily highs on Tuesday, according to Lunde.

Bitcoin touched $62,000 on Sunday, with investors realizing losses on a scale last seen near the lows of 2022 and early 2023, according to analysts at Glassnode. Short-term holders added about 66,000 BTC to their holdings in the $62,000 to $66,000 range during the two days of heaviest selling, Glassnode said.

Bitcoin traded at a premium to the global price on Coinbase near Sunday's low after spending most of the previous few weeks at a discount. Glassnode said a consistent premium would be a sign of sustained U.S. buying, though the discount had returned by Tuesday. On Binance, the largest concentration of buy orders at a single price since August sits near $60,000, though traders can pull those orders before they get filled.

Glassnode said a daily close below $62,000 would put the August buyers at a loss, with a large cluster of long liquidations beneath, opening the path to revisiting the June low near $58,500 and the Realized Price, the average price at which circulating bitcoin last moved onchain, at $53,700.

Meanwhile, in a note to clients on Tuesday, Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan traced the selloff to a sharp shift in Fed rate expectations. After the Nov. 10 report showed U.S. consumer prices rose a hotter-than-expected 0.4% in October, traders went from pricing in a 66% chance of a 25bps hike in December to treating it as a certainty, Hougan said, adding that thin weekend trading made the drop worse as roughly $2 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated.

Hougan also noted that the Crypto Fear and Greed Index, a gauge of crypto market sentiment, fell to 12 over the weekend, below its reading at bitcoin's June low.

"That’s good news, in a way. Because when you know why markets are falling, you can check whether the cause has played out. And in this case, I think it has," Hougan said. "Markets have now priced in aggressive rate hikes, and a lot of leverage has been flushed out."

#4992. Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold roughly $85 million worth of Nvidia shares Monday while buying close to $40 million in crypto-exposed stocks, rebalancing exposure to technology and fintech stocks during a broad selloff.

The firm's daily trade file for November 16 shows sales of 543,092 Nvidia shares across two actively managed exchange-traded funds. Using Monday's $156.14 closing price, those shares were worth approximately $84.8 million; the disclosures list share counts rather than the exact prices ARK received.

ARK bought 277,523 shares of payments company Block, worth about $23 million at the close. It also added 180,534 shares of stablecoin issuer Circle, valued at $10.4 million, and 53,760 shares of crypto exchange Coinbase, worth around $6.4 million.

The purchases were spread across funds rather than concentrated in one vehicle. ARK's flagship Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought Circle and most of the Block shares, while its Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW) bought Coinbase and the remaining Block stock.

All three crypto-linked stocks fell Monday. Circle dropped 7.3%, Coinbase declined 6.1% and Block lost 1.9%, while Nvidia slid 4.1% as investors continued selling technology shares.

That makes the whole movement seem like a shift in holdings, not evidence that ARK expects cryptocurrencies to recover before AI stocks. The manager says its funds can rebalance every trading day, and its trade notifications don't disclose why each position was changed or establish that particular sales financed particular purchases.

ARK had bought 90,443 Nvidia shares just one week earlier, on November 9, during another selloff. The latest sale therefore reverses some of that buying without necessarily suggesting the firm has abandoned the chipmaker or its long-standing investment case for artificial intelligence.

ARK also purchased 378,515 shares of SpaceX, worth roughly $52 million, while selling 30,659 shares of crypto exchange Bullish and units of Ethereum and Solana staking funds. So in this case, Wood would be selling crypto to buy one single AI stock.

Those sales included 300,000 shares of the 3iQ Ethereum Staking ETF and 350,000 shares of the 3iQ Solana Staking ETF. The firm's buying of crypto companies coincided with cuts to other crypto-related investments, a distinction that matters when trying to read a trading strategy from one day's activity.

Wood has repeatedly bought companies that handle crypto trading and payments during market selloffs. In September, ARK bought $37 million in Block stock in one session, and it previously increased its Circle and Coinbase stakes while reducing exposure to other crypto names.

The companies offer different ways to invest in digital assets without holding tokens directly. Block runs Cash App and Bitcoin-related products; Circle issues the USDC dollar-backed stablecoin; and Coinbase, the only American crypto exchange listed on the stock market, earns revenue from cryptocurrency trading and other services.

ARK's strategy has never been a simple choice between crypto and AI. Its flagship fund already counted Circle, Coinbase and SpaceX among major positions in August, alongside businesses tied to artificial intelligence and financial technology, as earlier holdings showed.

Nvidia's leadership changed five days before Monday's trades. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 11, with finance chief Colette Kress appointed interim chief executive, according to the company's SEC filing.

The chipmaker is due to report fiscal third-quarter results after the market closes Tuesday, with a conference call at 5 p.m. Eastern. Those results will give investors their first earnings update since the leadership change—one day after ARK sold more than half a million shares.

#4991. WNBA Star Gabby Williams Found a Team That Asked What She Wanted. Then She Won a Championship

The 30-year-old shares her philosophy on work-life balance and how she keeps her body strong and healthy on a new episode of The Huddle.

WNBA superstar Gabby Williams is proof that hard work and persistence pay off. Drafted into the league in 2018 by the Chicago Sky, the 30-year-old has been slowly building her résumé ever since—both stateside and abroad—notching her first EuroLeague championship in 2022 with Hungary’s Sopron Basket, being named a WNBA All-Star in 2025, and, finally, winning a WNBA Championship in 2026 with the Golden State Valkyries. (She was named Finals MVP too.)

Yes, 2026 has been a big year for the forward, and she has only a couple more months to rest up before taking on her next challenge: debuting in the Unrivaled league, as part of the Miami-based Laces BC.

“It's three-on-three, so you can't hide,” Gabby tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “The positive feedback that I've heard from people who have done it, [is] that the personal development side is great. Players usually go on to have great W seasons after doing Unrivaled.”

How could Gabby possibly top this past year!? We’ll have to wait to find out, but in the meantime, she opens up about finding a home with the Valkyries, keeping herself healthy and injury-free, and building a life outside of basketball.

Over the years, Gabby has earned the nickname “the French Army knife,” due not only to her dual-citizenship (her dad is American; her mom is French) but also to her versatility on the court.

Her role on many teams has been defined by what the team needed, whether it was creating opportunities or defending the paint. But when she went into free agency and signed with the Valkyries earlier this year, it was the first time Gabby recalls someone in the league asking what she wanted to do.

“I was proud to do whatever the team needed,” Gabby says. “But it was nice to trust myself.” That trust—both in herself and from her team—has obviously paid off. Not only does Gabby say she feels more like herself than she ever has, but she has the championship (the Valkyries’ first) to show for it.

Given how little downtime Gabby takes—she often spends part of her off-season playing abroad—she’s crafted a wellness routine that prioritizes stretching, mobility, and maintenance to keep her body in peak physical condition.

And it starts first thing when she wakes up. “I'm a big foam-roller stretcher, especially as I'm getting older,” she says. “I'll spend a good like 20, 15 minutes first thing in the morning just doing my mobility stuff so that when I come to the gym my body's awake and ready.”

At the gym, Gabby and her trainers prioritize accessory work over big Olympic lifts, to limit the wear and tear on her body.

In the off-season, Gabby shifts from a maintenance mindset to an improvement focus with her workouts. If she wants to strengthen a particular body part or movement pattern (like being more explosive) this is when she has the time and energy to do it.

No matter her training regimen, Gabby ends her day much like she starts it—with recovery. She loves an epsom salt bath and can’t get enough of her Normatec compression therapy.

It might be surprising to hear a WNBA champion say “basketball is not life,” but that’s precisely Gabby’s philosophy when it comes to balancing her priorities.

“I think that's why I've been able to have so much success in basketball is because I've learned how to compartmentalize,” she says. She credits that mindset to the coaching team at the University of Connecticut, where she played in college.

“Coach said, ‘When you're on the court, I want you to be focused. I don't want you to be thinking about school. I don't want you to be thinking about your personal life. So while you're doing your other stuff, don't focus on basketball as much. Find the time for your school. When you're going out, go out, have fun.’”

And so Gabby does just that, whether it’s solving a puzzle or picking up a new book. “It is just the perfect way to consume your mind with something else,” she says of reading. She’s even started a Valkyries book club, but it got a bit sidetracked by, of all things, the playoffs. Luckily, there’s always the 2027 season to start anew.

To hear more from Gabby, including her undying love of figure skating and how she’s upped her style game, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#4990. Maple Finance CEO targets up to $15B in assets by the end of 2027

Sidney Powell aims to reach $15 billion in assets under management by the end of 2027 as the firm looks to expand into tokenized lending and traditional finance.

Onchain asset manager Maple Finance is aiming to grow its assets under management (AUM) to between $10 billion and $15 billion by the end of 2027 as it looks to attract more traditional financial (TradFi) firms, according to CEO Sidney Powell.

In an exclusive interview with Cointelegraph on Monday, Powell said the company is also targeting a loan book of around $4.5 billion to $5 billion.

The plans come as Maple looks to grow beyond lending backed primarily by cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC) and attract more traditional financial firms, with Powell expecting tokenized assets and stablecoins to play a major role in the company’s growth.

Maple reported $4.7 billion in AUM at the end of the third quarter, up 18% from a year earlier. However, Maple’s dashboard showed around $3.9 billion in AUM on Tuesday.

Outstanding loans rose 12% from a year earlier to $1.7 billion, while quarterly revenue increased 5% to $4.4 million, bringing annualized revenue to $17.6 million. Still, outstanding loans fell 9% from the previous quarter, while quarterly revenue remained flat.

Tokenized assets are digital versions of traditional assets, such as stocks and bonds, that can be held and traded on a blockchain. Separately, stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset, most commonly a currency such as the US dollar.

The market for tokenized real-world assets has grown significantly over the past year, with their value on public blockchains reaching about $39.9 billion as of Nov. 11, up 52% year-over-year, according to RWA.xyz. The value of tokenized stocks alone rose from about $678 million in January to nearly $3.9 billion in November.

Maple assets under management. Source: Maple Finance

Powell expects tokenized stocks to grow fivefold to tenfold in 2027, which could allow Maple to offer loans backed by tokenized shares rather than relying mainly on cryptocurrency collateral.

“I think tokenized equities are going to be really big,” he said. “You’ll start to see more tokenized equity lending.”

Under this model, borrowers could use tokenized stocks as collateral to obtain loans without having to sell their investments, similar to how Bitcoin-backed lending works today.

“Ultimately, that’s really positive for the space because it gives you tokenized assets to lend against that are not correlated with Bitcoin,” Powell said. Bitcoin is the largest cryptocurrency with a market capitalization of over $1.28 trillion as of Nov. 17.

Maple is also discussing credit facilities through which banks would finance its Bitcoin-backed lending, Powell said.

“At the moment, we’re looking at a first deal where we’re speaking with banks about warehouse facilities for the Bitcoin-backed lending, so they would be a funder to us,” Powell said.

Maple already provides financing for a warehouse facility supporting Kraken’s crypto-backed lending program, which was announced in June. The proposed bank arrangements would instead bring funding into Maple’s lending business.

Powell added that Maple could pursue separate deals with US banks and lenders involving loans originated by TradFi institutions and subsequently brought onto blockchain networks. “I think that’s going to be a big market for 2027,” he said.

Maple outlined plans in September to lend against portfolios of asset-backed and mortgage-backed securities and finance loans originated by fintech companies. It said at the time that each new strategy would initially be capped at 5% of its overall deposit base.

Another priority is expanding partnerships with financial technology companies and digital banks that want to offer customers ways to earn interest on their stablecoin holdings. Powell said Maple is already in discussions with several large firms about potential products, with announcements possible in the first quarter of 2027.

“My view is that’s the kind of path Maple has to go down in order to grow, and we have to focus more on these larger institutional allocators,” Powell said. “That’s ultimately where most of the balance sheet is in traditional finance.”

That approach to expansion is also at the center of a leadership disagreement, according to Powell.

Related: Arch Lending eyes tokenized stocks as next collateral market

Maple’s growth plans come amid a leadership shakeup after co-founder and executive chairman Joe Flanagan and chief operating officer Ryan O’Shea announced plans last week to leave over disagreements about the company’s future direction.

Flanagan said his differences with Powell involved strategy and leadership, while O’Shea said he had reached a different view on the direction Maple should take.

Powell said the differences centered on how best to expand the business, particularly as TradFi institutions become more involved in crypto lending.

“We had a difference of opinion on the best way to scale things,” he told Cointelegraph. “This year, I think, more than ever, we started to see that real convergence with traditional finance, fintechs and neobanks. And my view is that that is kind of the right path for us to scale.”

The planned departures prompted questions from Maple’s investors, partners and clients, some of whom contacted Powell seeking clarification. Powell said the departures were unrelated to problems with Maple’s loan book or the health of the business.

“The important thing is conveying to them and reassuring them that this wasn’t to do with any issues in Maple’s loan book or any issues with the business,” Powell said. “It is just a difference on what is the best pathway to scale Maple from here.”

Maple Finance’s native token, SYRUP is currently trading at $0.103 as of 6:50 pm UTC on Tuesday, with a market capitalization of $123 million, according to CoinMarketCap. The token is down about 46% over the past 30 days and 74% over the past year.

#4989. StoneX cuts Bitdeer price target to $15 amid new US chip export controls

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

StoneX lowered its 2027 revenue and adjusted EBITDA forecasts for Bitdeer after the U.S. announced new chip export controls.

StoneX Financial analyst Mark Palmer cut his price target on Bitdeer Technologies Group Bitdeer Technologies Group (BTDR) to $15 from $22, but kept his Buy rating on the stock.

Bitdeer shares closed at $4 on Tuesday, down nearly 29% from Friday's close, according to StoneX. The firm's new target implies roughly 275% upside from that level.

In a note to clients on Wednesday, Palmer said new U.S. licensing requirements for advanced chip shipments to Malaysia raised questions about the timing of Bitdeer’s GPU deliveries. Nvidia GB300 systems for its new Malaysian sites were scheduled to start arriving this month, according to Palmer.

"BTDR is a company funding a capital-intensive transition from a low-margin bitcoin mining business with a levered balance sheet, which is why the durability of its AI-driven revenue matters so much," Palmer wrote. "That durability is what the new chip export rule has called into question."

Bitdeer reported record third-quarter revenue of $320.7 million, up 89% from a year earlier. The company's AI cloud business ended the quarter with $86 million in annualized recurring revenue and about $2.9 billion in contracted revenue backlog, most of which was tied to two Malaysian facilities, according to the note.

According to the note, StoneX now sees three possible outcomes for the Malaysia business. The firm assigned a 40% probability to licenses being granted or the capacity being leased to other customers after a one-quarter delay.

The firm also sees another 35% probability for a two- to three-quarter delay plus a 15% pricing concession. In its most adverse scenario, which carries a 25% probability, Bitdeer’s A201 project would not go ahead, and its existing GPU fleet would face limits and some customer losses.

"We do not think the right response to BTDR’s Malaysian challenge would be to assume the worst for the company or, for that matter, to pretend nothing in its story has changed," Palmer said.

Based on the revised assumptions, StoneX lowered its 2027 revenue forecast by about $230 million to $1.77 billion and its adjusted EBITDA forecast by about $150 million to $616.5 million.
